title: Is the smallest angle always a factor of 360?
description: Two statements are tested: every figure has the full turn as an angle of symmetry, and a whole-number smallest angle is a factor of the full turn. The smallest angle is added again and again until it reaches the full turn. Keeko's doubt is that any whole number can be the smallest angle.
teaching_notes: One idea: the full turn is always an angle of symmetry, and it is a multiple of the smallest angle, so a whole-number smallest angle must divide 360 exactly. Watch for students who think any whole number can be the smallest angle.

source: True or False: (1) Every figure will have 360 degrees as an
video_script.why: The child decides two statements about the full turn and the smallest angle of symmetry, and sees why a whole-number smallest angle divides 360.
video_script.substitution: a figure turned about its dot, with the smallest angle added again and again round a circle of 360 degrees
video_script.anchor: a figure with a dot at its centre, and a circle of three hundred sixty degrees round the dot
video_script.wrong_answer: any whole number can be the smallest angle
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko picks twenty five degrees as the smallest angle and does not check that the steps reach the full turn.
maths_rules: a full turn of 360° brings every figure back to itself, so 360° is always an angle of symmetry
the angles of symmetry are multiples of the smallest angle, so 360° is a multiple of the smallest angle
so the smallest angle fits a whole number of times in 360°, and a whole-number smallest angle is a factor of 360
example: 45° x 8 = 360°, so 45 is a factor of 360
25 x 14 = 350 and 25 x 15 = 375, so steps of 25° jump over 360°; 360 ÷ 25 is not a whole number, so 25° cannot be the smallest angle
video_script.design: A figure turned a full turn, then the smallest angle added again and again round a circle. Forty five degrees lands exactly on the full turn. Keeko's doubt is that any whole number can be the smallest angle.
